title: Antennae Galaxies composite of ALMA and Hubble observations
caption: The Antennae Galaxies, imaged by ALMA and the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: Antennae Galaxies, NGC 4038, NGC 4039 · constellation Corvus · about 75 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: ALMA (ESO/NAOJ/NRAO). Visible light image: the NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: Ranked #34 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: Red, pink and yellow clouds are laid over a blue visible-light picture of two colliding galaxies. These are the Antennae Galaxies, NGC 4038 and 4039, a pair of distorted spirals about 70 million light-years away in Corvus, the Crow. The blue comes from the Hubble Space Telescope and shows newborn stars, while the warmer colors come from ALMA.

ALMA picks up the clouds of dense, cold gas where new stars form, which visible light cannot show. It was tuned to pick up carbon monoxide molecules, which reveal otherwise invisible hydrogen clouds. Big concentrations of gas sit in the hearts of both galaxies and also in the chaotic zone where they collide. In the collision zone the gas adds up to billions of times the Sun's mass, a reservoir for future stars.
The ALMA data came from early testing, mostly with only twelve antennas placed close together. Even so, this was the best submillimeter-wavelength image ever taken of the pair.
scale: The source lists a distance of 75 million light years, so the light in this picture set out roughly 75 million years ago.

understand.summary: Visible light from Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys appears mainly in blue, while ALMA's millimeter and submillimeter observations (bands 3 and 7) are shown in red, pink and yellow.

explore: Longer wavelengths make sharp images harder to obtain, so here the Hubble picture remains the benchmark for resolution. Once the full ALMA array is completed, its vision is expected to be up to ten times sharper than Hubble's. Observations like these should help explain how galaxy collisions trigger the birth of new stars.
